It is located at the C-terminal end in ribosomal RNA methyltransferase B (RsmB, Sun, Fmu) and Nop2 and towards the N-terminal in RsmF. Escherichia coli RsmB methylates cytosine C967 in 16S rRNA [[cite:PUB00072551]]. RsmF is a multi-site-specific methyltransferase [[cite:PUB00055250]]. Nop2 methylates cytosine C2870 in the 25S rRNA of S. cerevisiae [[cite:PUB00072550]] and is critical for 60S biogenesis [[cite:PUB00014219]].

Name: RNA (C5-cytosine) methyltransferase
ShortDescription:
RNA (C5-cytosine) methyltransferases (RCMTs) catalyse the transfer of a methyl group to the 5th carbon of a cytosine base in RNA sequences to produce C5-methylcytosine. RCMTs use the cofactor S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) as a methyl donor [[cite:PUB00054125]]. The catalytic mechanism of RCMTs involves an attack by the thiolate of a Cys residue on position 6 of the target cytosine base to form a covalent link, thereby activating C5 for methyl-group transfer. Following the addition of the methyl group, a second Cys residue acts as a general base in the beta-elimination of the proton from the methylated cytosine ring. The free enzyme is restored and the methylated product is released [[cite:PUB00054126]].

Numerous putative RCMTs have been identified in archaea, bacteria and eukaryota [[cite:PUB00014205], [cite:PUB00054127]]; most are predicted to be nuclear or nucleolar proteins [[cite:PUB00054128]]. The Escherichia coli Ribosomal RNA Small-subunit Methyltransferase Beta (RSMB) FMU (FirMicUtes) represents the first protein identified and characterised as a cytosine-specific RNA methyltransferase. RSMB was reported to catalyse the formation of C5-methylcytosine at position 967 of 16S rRNA [[cite:PUB00054129], [cite:PUB00014203]].

A classification of RCMTs has been proposed on the basis of sequence similarity [[cite:PUB00014205]]. According to this classification, RCMTs are divided into 8 distinct subfamilies [[cite:PUB00014205]]. Recently, a new RCMT subfamily, termed RCMT9, was identified [[cite:PUB00054127]]. Members of the RCMT contain a core domain, responsible for the cytosine-specific RNA methyltransferase activity. This 'catalytic' domain adopts the Rossman fold for the accommodation of the cofactor SAM [[cite:PUB00054130]]. The RCMT subfamilies are also distinguished by N-terminal and C-terminal extensions, variable both in size and sequence [[cite:PUB00014205]].

Name: RNA-binding protein Musashi homologue, RNA recognition motif 2
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the RNA recognition motif 2 (RRM2) of Musashi-1, which is a highly conserved RNA binding protein that was initially identified in Drosophila by its ability to regulate sensory organ development and asymmetric cell division [[cite:PUB00082719]]. Mammalian Musashi-1 has multiple functions in normal and abnormal processes by mediating different post-transcriptional processes. It has been implicated in the maintenance of the stem-cell state, differentiation, and tumorigenesis. It translationally regulates the expression of a mammalian numb gene by binding to the 3'-untranslated region of mRNA of Numb, encoding a membrane-associated inhibitor of Notch signaling, and further influences neural development [[cite:PUB00082722]]. Moreover, Musashi-1 represses translation by interacting with the poly(A)-binding protein and competes for binding of the eukaryotic initiation factor-4G (eIF-4G) [[cite:PUB00082721]].

Proteins containing this domain also includes Musashi-2, which has been identified as a regulator of the hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) compartment and of leukemic stem cells after transplantation of cells with loss and gain of function of the gene [[cite:PUB00082724]]. It influences proliferation and differentiation of HSCs and myeloid progenitors, and further modulates normal hematopoiesis and promotes aggressive myeloid leukemia [[cite:PUB00082725], [cite:PUB00082723]]. Musashi-1 and Musashi-2 contain two conserved N-terminal tandem RNA recognition motifs (RRMs), also termed RBDs (RNA binding domains) or RNPs (ribonucleoprotein domains), along with other domains of unknown function

Name: Protein Spindly, chordates
ShortDescription: Protein Spindly is required for the localisation of dynein and dynactin to the mitotic kintochore [[cite:PUB00044111]]. It is required for silencing the spindle assembly checkpoint [[cite:PUB00044111], [cite:PUB00089926]]. It localises to microtubule plus ends in interphase and to kinetochores during mitosis [[cite:PUB00068812]]. The localisation of human Spindly (hSpindly) to kinetochore-microtubules is controlled by the Rod/Zw10/Zwilch (RZZ) complex and Aurora B [[cite:PUB00068812], [cite:PUB00068813]].

Name: Spindly/BICDR Dynein Motor Adapter
ShortDescription: The Spindly/BICDR protein family is involved in the regulation of dynein motor activity and cargo transport [[cite:PUB00156756], [cite:PUB00161831], [cite:PUB00161832]]. Spindly proteins are essential for the localisation of dynein and dynactin to the mitotic kinetochore, controlling the interaction between the kinetochore and spindle microtubules and facilitating the formation of end-on kinetochore-microtubule attachments via the NDC80 complex [[cite:PUB00044111], [cite:PUB00068812], [cite:PUB00147713]]. They act as adapter proteins, linking dynein to various cargos and enhancing dynein processivity, which is crucial for long-distance movement along microtubules. Additionally, they play roles in correct spindle orientation, cell migration, and neurite outgrowth by regulating secretory vesicle transport in developing neurons.

Name: SAAL1, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the C-terminal domain of the Synoviocyte proliferation-associated in collagen-induced arthritis protein 1 (SAAL1) and related proteins. SAAL1 is a nuclear protein found in vertebrates that plays a role in promoting cell proliferation in response to pro-inflammatory stimuli [[cite:PUB00162285]]. The full-length protein promotes the proliferation of synovial fibroblasts and is expressed in testis, ovary, and synovial tissue of knee joints. The specific function of this C-terminal domain remains to be determined.

Name: Synovial Proliferation Regulator
ShortDescription: This family of proteins is involved in cellular responses to inflammatory stimuli. Members of this family are known to contribute to the proliferation of cells, particularly synovial fibroblasts, under such conditions. The role of these proteins is crucial in the regulation of inflammatory processes and may have implications in various physiological and pathological states where inflammation is a key factor.

Name: Sphingosine N-acyltransferase Lag1/Lac1-like
ShortDescription:
Yeast ceramide synthase component Lag1 has a paralog, Lac1. This entry includes Lac1, Lag1 and their homologues from plants and animals [[cite:PUB00073472], [cite:PUB00073471], [cite:PUB00097253]], involved in sphingolipid synthesis.

LAG1 and LAC1 contain multiple membrane-spanning domains and are localised to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) [[cite:PUB00073468]]. They are essential subunits of the acyl-CoA-dependent ceramide synthase that is involved in synthesis of ceramide from C26(acyl)-coenzyme A and dihydrosphingosine or phytosphingosine [[cite:PUB00073469], [cite:PUB00073470], [cite:PUB00009697]].

Human Lac1/Lag1 homologue CERS2 (ceramide synthase 2) is a tumour metastasis suppressor that can inhibit breast cancer cell invasion [[cite:PUB00073765]].

Name: TRAM/LAG1/CLN8 homology domain
ShortDescription: TLC is a protein domain with at least 5 transmembrane α-helices. Lag1p and Lac1p are essential for acyl-CoA-dependent ceramide synthesis [[cite:PUB00009697]], TRAM is a subunit of the translocon and the CLN8 gene is mutated in Northern epilepsy syndrome. Proteins containing this domain may possess multiple functions such as lipid trafficking, metabolism, or sensing. Trh homologues possess additional homeobox domains [[cite:PUB00008436]].

Name: Zinc finger, CCCH-type
ShortDescription:
This entry represents C-x8-C-x5-C-x3-H (CCCH) type Zinc finger (Znf) domains.

;

Proteins containing CCCH Znf domains include Znf proteins from eukaryotes involved in cell cycle or growth phase-related regulation, e.g. human TIS11B (butyrate response factor 1, also known as mRNA decay activator protein ZFP36L1), a probable regulatory protein involved in regulating the response to growth factors, and the mouse TTP growth factor-inducible nuclear protein, which has the same function. The mouse TTP protein is induced by growth factors. Another protein containing this domain is the human splicing factor U2AF 35kDa subunit, which plays a critical role in both constitutive and enhancer-dependent splicing by mediating essential protein-protein interactions and protein-RNA interactions required for 3' splice site selection. It has been shown that different CCCH-type Znf proteins interact with the 3'-untranslated region of various mRNA [[cite:PUB00005945], [cite:PUB00005946]]. This type of Znf is very often present in two copies.

;

Zinc finger (Znf) domains are relatively small protein motifs which contain multiple finger-like protrusions that make tandem contacts with their target molecule. Some of these domains bind zinc, but many do not; instead, they bind other metals, such as iron, or no metal at all. For example, some family members form salt bridges to stabilise the finger-like folds. They were first identified as a DNA-binding motif in transcription factor TFIIIA from Xenopus laevis (African clawed frog); however, they are now recognised to bind DNA, RNA, protein and/or lipid substrates [[cite:PUB00035807], [cite:PUB00035805], [cite:PUB00035806], [cite:PUB00035804], [cite:PUB00014077]]. Their binding properties depend on the amino acid sequence of the finger domains and of the linker between fingers, as well as on the higher-order structures and the number of fingers. Znf domains are often found in clusters, where fingers can have different binding specificities. There are many superfamilies of Znf motifs, varying in both sequence and structure. They display considerable versatility in binding modes, even between members of the same class (e.g., some bind DNA, others protein), suggesting that Znf motifs are stable scaffolds that have evolved specialised functions. For example, Znf-containing proteins function in gene transcription, translation, mRNA trafficking, cytoskeleton organisation, epithelial development, cell adhesion, protein folding, chromatin remodelling and zinc sensing, to name but a few [[cite:PUB00035812]]. Zinc-binding motifs are stable structures, and they rarely undergo conformational changes upon binding their target.

Name: CAF1 family poly(A)-specific ribonucleases
ShortDescription: The CAF1 family proteins are specialized 3'-exoribonucleases with a preference for degrading poly(A) tails of mRNAs, a key step in eukaryotic mRNA decay. They play roles in various biological processes including translational silencing of maternal mRNAs during oocyte maturation and early embryonic development, nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, and the degradation of unstable mRNAs with AU-rich elements. Some family members are also involved in the maturation and processing of snRNAs, piRNAs, and the regulation of microRNAs and small nucleolar RNAs. Their functions are critical for cell growth regulation, fertility, gene silencing, and stress response.

Name: Ribonuclease CAF1
ShortDescription:
The major pathways of mRNA turnover in eukaryotes initiate with shortening of the poly(A) tail. CAF1 (also known as CCR4-associated factor 1) is an RNase of the DEDD superfamily, and a subunit of the CCR4-NOT complex that mediates 3' to 5' mRNA deadenylation [[cite:PUB00082305], [cite:PUB00082306]]. In yeast, CAF1 ([swissprot:P39008]) is also known as POP2, and encodes a critical component of the major cytoplasmic deadenylase [[cite:PUB00082302], [cite:PUB00019239]]. It is required for normal mRNA deadenylationin vivoand localises to the cytoplasm. CAF1 copurifies with a CCR4-dependent poly(A)-specific exonuclease activity. The crystal structure of Saccharomyces cerevisiae POP2 has been resolved [[cite:PUB00019241]].

Some members of this family contain a single-stranded nucleic acid binding domain, R3H, such as poly(A)-specific ribonuclease (PARN), which also contains an RRM domain [[cite:PUB00082307]]. PARN is only conserved in vertebrates and may be important in regulated deadenylation such as early developmentand DNA damage response [[cite:PUB00082309], [cite:PUB00082310]].

Name: Dilute domain
ShortDescription:
The myosin superfamily consists of at least 15 distinct classes of presumed actin-based molecular motors. All members of the superfamily share a similar motor domain and a tail portion which is diagnostic of the class [[cite:PUB00015330]].

Class V myosins are actin-based molecular motors that function in relatively long-range movements of many intracellular cargoes including organelles, membrane vesicles, and mRNA [[cite:PUB00018557]]. These motors are ubiquitously found in all eukaryotes. Class V myosins are characterised by the presence of a conserved globular domain at the C terminus of the tail portion: the dilute domain [[cite:PUB00005744]]. Myosin V moves via attachment of its amino terminal head (motor) domain to actin cables; its carboxyl terminal dilute domain anchors it to cargoes via attachments to organelle-specific receptors [[cite:PUB00018557], [cite:PUB00018558]].

The dilute domain is also found in the afadin family. Afadins are nectin and actin filament-binding proteins that connect nectin to the actin cytoskeleton [[cite:PUB00018559]]. The dilute domain of afadin appears to be responsible for actin stress fibre formation [[cite:PUB00078822]].

Name: Rasip1/Radil, cargo-binding domain
ShortDescription:
Ras-interacting protein 1 (Rasip1 or RAIN) is an effector of the small G protein Rap1 and plays an important role in endothelial junction stabilization [[cite:PUB00087997], [cite:PUB00087998], [cite:PUB00087999]]. It plays an essential role in vascular development [[cite:PUB00088002]].

Radil is also a Rap1 effector. It regulates beta1 and beta2-integrin activation and controls neutrophil chemotaxis [[cite:PUB00088003]]. Radil, like Rasip1, is a multi domain protein, that contains a myosin5-like cargo-binding domain (CBD).

Name: Vascular development regulator domain-containing protein
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes members that are involved in the regulation of GTPase signaling pathways, particularly in the context of vascular development and endothelial cell function. They play a crucial role in the formation of vascular structures through vasculogenesis and angiogenesis. These proteins modulate the activity of Rho GTPases, which are key regulators of cell architecture and adhesion, thereby influencing endothelial cell morphogenesis and tubulogenesis of blood vessels. Some family members act as downstream effectors of Ras and Rap proteins, impacting processes such as cell adhesion, migration, and possibly transformation. Additionally, certain proteins in this family have been implicated as negative regulators of autophagy under conditions of amino acid starvation.

Name: DNA binding HTH domain, Psq-type
ShortDescription: The psq-type HTH domain is a DNA-binding, helix-turn-helix (HTH) domain of about 50 amino acids present in eukaryotic proteins of the Pipsqueak family. This family is named after the Drosophila pipsqueak protein, containing a DNA-binding domain that consists of four tandem repeats of the psq motif [[cite:PUB00010427]]. Proteins of the Pipsqueak family occur in vertebrates, insects, nematodes, and fungi.

Name: PX domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
The PX (phox) domain [[cite:PUB00005042]] occurs in a variety of eukaryotic proteins and has been implicated in highly diverse functions, including cell signalling, vesicular trafficking, protein sorting and lipid modification [[cite:PUB00020791], [cite:PUB00020788], [cite:PUB00010010], [cite:PUB00084390]]. PX domains are important phosphoinositide-binding modules that exhibit varying lipid-binding specificities [[cite:PUB00007152]]. The PX domain is approximately 120 residues in length [[cite:PUB00008032]] and folds into a three-stranded β-sheet followed by three α-helices and a proline-rich region. This region immediately precedes a membrane-interaction loop and spans approximately eight hydrophobic and polar residues. The PX domain of neutrophil cytosol factor 1 (p47phox) binds to the SH3 domain within the same protein [[cite:PUB00008032]]. Phosphorylation of p47(phox), a cytoplasmic activator of the microbicidal phagocyte oxidase (phox), triggers interaction of p47(phox) with phosphoinositides. This phosphorylation-driven conformational change enables the PX domain to bind phosphoinositides, an interaction that plays a crucial role in the recruitment of p47(phox) from the cytoplasm to membranes and subsequent activation of the phagocyte oxidase. The lipid-binding activity of this protein is normally suppressed by intramolecular interaction between the PX domain and the C-terminal Src homology 3 (SH3) domain [[cite:PUB00011220]].

The PX domain is conserved from yeast to humans. Multiple alignment of representative PX domain sequences from eukaryotic proteins [[cite:PUB00006581]] reveals relatively little sequence conservation, although the overall structure appears to be highly conserved. While phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate (PtdIns(3)P) is the primary target of PX domains, binding to phosphatidic acid, phosphatidylinositol-3,4-bisphosphate (PtdIns(3,4)P2), phosphatidylinositol-3,5-bisphosphate (PtdIns(3,5)P2), phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PtdIns(4,5)P2) and phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate (PtdIns(3,4,5)P3) has also been reported. The PX domain additionally functions as a protein-protein interaction domain [[cite:PUB00020786]].

This domain is found in Sorting nexin and related proteins. Sorting nexins (SNXs) are a diverse family of proteins characterised by the presence of a phosphoinositide-binding PX domain, which mediates their association with endosomal membranes. They play essential roles in membrane trafficking, endosomal sorting and signal transduction across eukaryotes.

SNX1 functions in retrograde transport from endosomes to the trans-Golgi network as a core component of the retromer complex, facilitating the retrieval of cargo receptors such as the cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor [[cite:PUB00068936]].

SNX2 shares functional similarity with SNX1 and also participates in retromer-mediated retrograde trafficking, with partial redundancy between the two proteins in endosome-to-Golgi transport [[cite:PUB00068936]].

SNX3 is a smaller sorting nexin that regulates the recycling of specific cargo proteins, including Wntless, which is essential for Wnt secretion [[cite:PUB00163290], [cite:PUB00163291]], and transferrin receptor, thereby contributing to iron homeostasis [[cite:PUB00163292]].

SNX4 is involved in endosomal recycling pathways, where it promotes transferrin receptor recycling and prevents its degradation [[cite:PUB00084407]], and additionally participates in autophagosome assembly by regulating the trafficking of the phospholipid scramblase ATG9A [[cite:PUB00101856], [cite:PUB00163293]].

Name: SNX27, RA domain
ShortDescription:
Sorting nexin-27 (SNX27) belongs to the sorting nexin family, which contains a conserved PX (phox homology) domain that may be responsible for binding to specific phosphoinositides [[cite:PUB00068935]]. SNX27 also possesses an PDZ (DHR) domain, a Ras-associating domain and a FERM-like domain with an atypical tertiary structure [[cite:PUB00068986]].

SNX27 is a core component of the SNX27-retromer, a multiprotein complex composed of SNX27, the WASH complex and the retromer complex. It specifically binds and directs sorting of a subset of transmembrane proteins containing a PDZ-binding motif at the C terminus [[cite:PUB00068992]]. Its PDZ domain mediates binding to the retromer complex via direct interaction with VPS26 (VPS26A or VPS26B) [[cite:PUB00068993]], while its PX domain mediates binding to phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PtdIns(3P)) and localization to early endosome membranes [[cite:PUB00068992]].

This entry represents the FERM-like domain of SNX27. This domain binds PtdInsPs in a manner that is distinct to that of distantly related FERM, pleckstrin homology (PH) and phosphotyrosine-binding (PTB) domains [[cite:PUB00087677]].

Name: Mitochondrial Inner Membrane Protease Subunit 1
ShortDescription: The Mitochondrial Inner Membrane Protease (IMP) Subunit 1 family comprises enzymes that play a crucial role in the maturation of mitochondrial proteins. Members of this family are responsible for catalyzing the removal of transit peptides from precursor proteins that are targeted from the mitochondrial matrix, across the inner membrane, into the inter-membrane space. This proteolytic process is essential for the proper functioning of the mitochondrial protein import machinery. Specific substrates for these proteases include nuclear-encoded proteins such as DIABLO, CYB2, and GUT2, as well as mitochondrially encoded proteins like COX2. The IMP1 subfamily belongs to the broader peptidase S26 family and includes both catalytic and non-catalytic components that may have distinct substrate specificities, ensuring a wide range of mitochondrial proteins are correctly processed and matured.

Name: Conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 8, Metazoal and Viridiplantae
ShortDescription: This entry represents conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 8 from metazoans and viridiplantae. It is a component of the peripheral membrane COG complex that is involved in intra-Golgi protein trafficking [[cite:PUB00009854]].

Name: Conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 8
ShortDescription: Conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 8 acts as component of the peripheral membrane COG complex that is involved in intra-Golgi protein trafficking [[cite:PUB00009854]].

Name: UAP56-interacting factor
ShortDescription: UAP56-interacting factor, also known as UIF, is a mRNA export adaptor that works together with adaptor REF/ALY. It is required for mRNA export from the nucleus to the cytoplasm [[cite:PUB00074858]].

Name: Exportin-6
ShortDescription: XPO6 is a nuclear export receptor that transfers profilin-actin complexes from the nucleus to the cytoplasm [[cite:PUB00090421]]. Reduced interaction of Exp6 and RanGTP has been linked to cellular senescence [[cite:PUB00090422]]. It mediates the nuclear export of actin and profilin-actin complexes in somatic cells [[cite:PUB00090421]].

Name: Cyclin-like domain
ShortDescription: This cyclin-like domain is found in cyclins, but it is also found as the core domain in transcription factor IIB (TFIIB) [[cite:PUB00022837]] and in the retinoblastoma tumour suppressor [[cite:PUB00049281]]. It consists of a duplication of a fold consisting of 5 helices, one of them surrounded by the others.

Name: Cyclin-like superfamily
ShortDescription: This cyclin-like domain superfamily is found in cyclins, but it is also found as the core domain in transcription factor IIB (TFIIB) [[cite:PUB00022837]] and in the retinoblastoma tumour suppressor [[cite:PUB00049281]]. It consists of a duplication of a fold consisting of 5 helices, one of them surrounded by the others.

Name: Cyclin, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription:
Cyclins are eukaryotic proteins that play an active role in controlling nuclear cell division cycles [[cite:PUB00014103]], and regulate cyclin dependent kinases (CDKs). Cyclins, together with the p34 (cdc2) or cdk2 kinases, form the Maturation Promoting Factor (MPF). There are two main groups of cyclins, G1/S cyclins, which are essential for the control of the cell cycle at the G1/S (start) transition, and G2/M cyclins, which are essential for the control of the cell cycle at the G2/M (mitosis) transition. G2/M cyclins accumulate steadily during G2 and are abruptly destroyed as cells exit from mitosis (at the end of the M-phase). In most species, there are multiple forms of G1 and G2 cyclins. For example, in vertebrates, there are two G2 cyclins, A and B, and at least three G1 cyclins, C, D, and E.

Cyclin homologues have been found in various viruses, including Saimiriine herpesvirus 2 (Herpesvirus saimiri) and Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) (Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus). These viral homologues differ from their cellular counterparts in that the viral proteins have gained new functions and eliminated others to harness the cell and benefit the virus [[cite:PUB00014101]].

This is the C-terminal domain of cyclins.

Name: Cyclin/Cyclin-like subunit Ssn8
ShortDescription:
Cyclins are eukaryotic proteins that play an active role in controlling nuclear cell division cycles, and regulate cyclin dependent kinases (CDKs) [[cite:PUB00014103]].

This entry represents several Cyclin families (C, L, Q, T1, T2, and H/Ccl1) and yeast RNA polymerase II holoenzyme cyclin-like subunit (also known as Ssn8/Srb11).

  • Cyclin C can regulate both cell cycle progression and gene transcription. The Cdk8-cyclin C complex is a component of the RNA polymerase II holoenzyme [[cite:PUB00055077]].
  • Cyclin L is a transcriptional regulator involved in the regulation of RNA polymerase II transcription and participating in regulating the pre-mRNA splicing process [[cite:PUB00034807], [cite:PUB00068054]].
  • Cyclin Q (also known as Cyclin M) consists of cyclin-related protein FAM58A [[cite:PUB00087326]].
  • Cyclin-T2 is a regulatory subunit of the cyclin-dependent kinase pair (CDK9/cyclin T) complex [[cite:PUB00016032]].
  • Cyclin-H from vertebrates, mcs2 from fission yeast and Ccl1 from budding yeasts are cyclins that play a role in cell cycle [[cite:PUB00069500]].

Name: Cyclin, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
Cyclins contain two domains of similar all-α fold, of which this entry is associated with the N-terminal domain.

;

Cyclins are eukaryotic proteins that play an active role in controlling nuclear cell division cycles [[cite:PUB00014103]], and regulate cyclin dependent kinases (CDKs). Cyclins, together with the p34 (cdc2) or cdk2 kinases, form the Maturation Promoting Factor (MPF). There are two main groups of cyclins, G1/S cyclins, which are essential for the control of the cell cycle at the G1/S (start) transition, and G2/M cyclins, which are essential for the control of the cell cycle at the G2/M (mitosis) transition. G2/M cyclins accumulate steadily during G2 and are abruptly destroyed as cells exit from mitosis (at the end of the M-phase). In most species, there are multiple forms of G1 and G2 cyclins. For example, in vertebrates, there are two G2 cyclins, A and B, and at least three G1 cyclins, C, D, and E.

Cyclin homologues have been found in various viruses, including Saimiriine herpesvirus 2 (Herpesvirus saimiri) and Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) (Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus). These viral homologues differ from their cellular counterparts in that the viral proteins have gained new functions and eliminated others to harness the cell and benefit the virus [[cite:PUB00014101]].

Name: KCTD15, tetramerisation-type BTB domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the BTB (Broad-Complex, Tramtrack and Bric a brac)/POZ (poxvirus and zinc finger) domain, also known as tetramerization (T1) domain, found in KCTD15 proteins from vertebrates. It is a versatile protein-protein interaction motif that facilitates homodimerization or heterodimerization. The BTB domains from KCTD family members can adopt a wide range of oligomerization geometries, including homodimerization, tetramerization, and pentamerization. The KCTD1 BTB domains, closely related to KCTD15, form pentamers [[cite:PUB00099269], [cite:PUB00099270]].

BTB/POZ domain-containing protein KCTD15 (potassium channel tetramerization domain-containing protein 15) plays a role in the regulation of neural crest (NC) formation and other steps in embryonic development. It inhibits AP2 transcriptional activity by interacting with its activation domain [[cite:PUB00099268], [cite:PUB00099266], [cite:PUB00099267]].

Name: BTB/POZ domain-containing protein KCTD1/15-like, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the C-terminal domain of BTB/POZ domain-containing proteins 1 and 15 (KCTD1/15), characterised by β-sheets surrounded by α-helices ([pdbe:6S4L]) [[cite:PUB00151636]]. Structural similarities of the C-terminal domain of KCTD proteins allowed their classification in clades and subclades described in [[cite:PUB00151636]]. This domain is also found in similar animal proteins.

Name: Methylthiotransferase, N-terminal
ShortDescription: The methylthiotransferase (MTTase) or miaB-like family is named after the (dimethylallyl)adenosine tRNA MTTase miaB protein, which catalyses a C-H to C-S bond conversion in the methylthiolation of tRNA. A related bacterial enzyme rimO performs a similar methylthiolation, but on a protein substrate. RimO acts on the ribosomal protein uS12 and forms a separate MTTase subfamily. The miaB-subfamily includes mammalian CDK5 regulatory subunit-associated proteins and similar proteins in other eukaryotes. Two other subfamilies, yqeV and CDKAL1, are named after a Bacillus subtilis and a human protein, respectively. While yqeV-like proteins are found in bacteria, CDKAL1 subfamily members occur in eukaryotes and in archaebacteria. The likely MTTases from these 4 subfamilies contain an N-terminal MTTase domain, a central radical generating fold and a C-terminal TRAM domain (see [prositedoc:PDOC50926]). The core forms a radical SAM fold (or AdoMet radical), containing a cysteine motif CxxxCxxC that binds a [4Fe-4S] cluster [[cite:PUB00009728], [cite:PUB00046148], [cite:PUB00010539]]. A reducing equivalent from the [4Fe-4S]+ cluster is used to cleave S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to generate methionine and a 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical. The latter is thought to produce a reactive substrate radical that is amenable to sulphur insertion [[cite:PUB00046148], [cite:PUB00010539]]. The N-terminal MTTase domain contains 3 cysteines that bind a second [4Fe-4S] cluster, in addition to the radical-generating [4Fe-4S] cluster, which could be involved in the thiolation reaction. The C-terminal TRAM domain is not shared with other radical SAM proteins outside the MTTase family. The TRAM domain can bind to RNA substrate and seems to be important for substrate recognition. The tertiary structure of the central radical SAM fold has six β/α motifs resembling a three-quarter TIM barrel core (see [prositedoc:PDOC00155]) [[cite:PUB00052321]]. The N-terminal MTTase domain might form an additional [β/α]2 TIM barrel unit [[cite:PUB00046148]].

Name: Radical SAM, alpha/beta horseshoe
ShortDescription:
Radical SAM domains catalyze diverse reactions, including unusual methylations, isomerization, sulphur insertion, ring formation, anaerobic oxidation and protein radical formation. Evidence exists that these proteins generate a radical species by reductive cleavage of S:-adenosylmethionine (SAM) through an unusual Fe-S centre [[cite:PUB00010539], [cite:PUB00015124]].

This entry represents radical SAM domains that form an α/β horseshoe structure [[cite:PUB00054243]].

Name: TRAM domain
ShortDescription:
The TRAM (after TRM2 and miaB) domain is a 60-70-residue-long module that is found in:

  • Two distinct classes of tRNA-modifying enzymes, namely uridine methylases of the TRM2 family and enzymes of the miaB family that are involved in 2- methylthioadenine formation
  • In several other proteins associated with the translation machinery
  • In a family of small archaeal proteins, including the RNA chaperone [swissprot:Q6M142] from Methanococcus maripaludis [[cite:PUB00158982]] and uncharacterised sequences that are predicted to have a role in the regulation of tRNA modification and/or translation

The TRAM domain can be found alone or in association with other domains, such as the catalytic biotin/lipoate synthetase-like domain, the RNA methylase domain, the ribosomal S2 domain and the eIF2-beta domain. The TRAM domain is predicted to bind tRNA and deliver the RNA-modifying enzymatic domain to their targets [[cite:PUB00009729]]. Secondary structure prediction indicates that the TRAM domain adopts a simple β-barrel fold. The conservation pattern of the TRAM domain consists primarily of small and hydrophobic residues that correspond to five β-strands in the predicted secondary structure [[cite:PUB00009729]].

Name: tRNA-2-methylthio-N(6)-dimethylallyladenosine synthase MiaB
ShortDescription: This entry represents the MiaB enzyme and homologues that are responsible for the modification of the isopentenylated adenine-37 base of most bacterial and eukaryotic tRNAs that read codons beginning with uracil (all except tRNA(I,V) Ser). Adenine-37 is next to the anticodon on the 3' side in these tRNA's, and lack of modification at this site leads to an increased spontaneous mutation frequency. Isopentenylated A-37 is modified by methylthiolation at position 2 leading to the formation of 2-methylthio-N6-(dimethylallyl)adenosine, either by MiaB alone or in concert with a separate methylase yet to be discovered [[cite:PUB00009727]]. MiaB contains two 4Fe-4S clusters which are labile under oxidizing conditions [[cite:PUB00009728], [cite:PUB00083447]]. One cluster is coordinated with three cysteines and an exchangeable S-adenosyl-L-methionine, the other is thought to be the sulfur donor. The second cluster has a polysulfide group bound to it, which is methylated in the first reaction step. Concurrently, the SAM-[4Fe-4S] cluster forms the 5'-dAdo radical, which abstracts a hydrogen atom from the substrate, which is then methylthiolated by the methylated polysulfide group [[cite:PUB00017717], [cite:PUB00083446], [cite:PUB00083448]]. Additionally, the sequence is homologous to the biotin synthetase, BioB, which utilises both an iron-sulfur cluster and S-adenosym methionine (SAM) to generate a radical which is responsible for initiating the insertion of sulfur into the substrate [[cite:PUB00009729]]. It is reasonable to surmise that the methyl group of SAM becomes the methyl group of the product, but this has not been shown, and the possibility of a separate methylase exists. These enzymes contain a TRAM domain [[cite:PUB00009729]] which is believed to be responsible for binding to tRNAs. The enzyme from Thermotoga maritima has been cloned, expressed, spectroscopically characterised and shown to complement the E. coli MiaB enzyme [[cite:PUB00017717]].

Name: Radical SAM superfamily
ShortDescription:
This superfamily represents the radical SAM domain, which is organised in a fold related to the β-barrel or TIM barrel, in which β-strands are arranged in a barrel-like array, with peripheral helices intervening between β-strands. The [4Fe-4S] clusters and substrates are bound within the barrels, as is typical of TIM barrel enzymes [[cite:PUB00097557], [cite:PUB00097556]].

;

Radical SAM proteins are found in all domains of life and share an unusual Fe-S cluster associated with generation of a free radical by reductive cleavage of SAM and often provide an anaerobic or oxygen-independent mechanism that is found as an aerobic reaction in other proteins. Radical SAM proteins catalyse diverse reactions, including unusual methylations, isomerisation, sulphur insertion, ring formation, anaerobic oxidation and protein radical formation. These proteins function in DNA precursor, vitamin, cofactor, antibiotic and herbicide biosynthesis and in biodegradation pathways [[cite:PUB00010539], [cite:PUB00015124]].

Radical SAM proteins share several common features, notably three strictly conserved cysteine residues generally included in the CxxxCxxC motif. These critical cysteines coordinate the unusual [4Fe-4S]2+/1+ cluster, while SAM serves as ligand for the fourth iron atom and acts as a cofactor or a cosubstrate [[cite:PUB00010539]]. The radical SAM enzymes biochemically characterised to date have in common the cleavage of the [4Fe-4S]1+-SAM complex to [4Fe-4S]2+-Met and the 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical, which abstracts a hydrogen atom from the substrate to initiate a radical mechanism [[cite:PUB00065909], [cite:PUB00097555]].

Name: Methylthiotransferase
ShortDescription:

The miaB-subfamily includes mammalian CDK5 regulatory subunit-associated proteins and similar proteins in other eukaryotes. Two other subfamilies, yqeV and CDKAL1, are named after a Bacillus subtilis and a human protein, respectively. While yqeV-like proteins are found in bacteria, CDKAL1 subfamily members occur in eukaryotes and in archaebacteria [[cite:PUB00083160]].

The likely MTTases from these 4 subfamilies contain an N-terminal MTTase domain, a central radical generating fold and a C-terminal TRAM domain (see [interpro:IPR002792]). The core forms a radical SAM fold (or AdoMet radical), containing a cysteine motif CxxxCxxC that binds a [4Fe-4S] cluster [[cite:PUB00009728], [cite:PUB00046148], [cite:PUB00010539]]. The C-terminal TRAM domain is not shared with other radical SAM proteins outside the MTTase family. The TRAM domain can bind to RNA substrate and seems to be important for substrate recognition. The tertiary structure of the central radical SAM fold has six β/α motifs resembling a three-quarter TIM barrel core [[cite:PUB00052321]]. The N-terminal MTTase domain might form an additional [β/α]2 TIM barrel unit [[cite:PUB00046148]].

Name: Elp3/MiaA/NifB-like, radical SAM core domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found in FeMo cofactor biosynthesis protein NifB, PqqA peptide cyclase, Oxygen-independent coproporphyrinogen III oxidase (HemN), biotin synthase (BioB), Lipoyl synthase (LipA), Ribosomal protein S12 methylthiotransferase RimO, GTP 3',8-cyclase (MoaA) and tRNA-2-methylthio-N(6)-dimethylallyladenosine synthase (MiaB), and similar proteins found in cellular organisms. This group includes a representative in the eukaryotic elongator subunit, Elp-3. Some members of this entry are methyltransferases [[cite:PUB00010539], [cite:PUB00101370]].

Name: Peptidase S26A, signal peptidase I, conserved site
ShortDescription:
Signal peptidases (SPases) [[cite:PUB00005393]] (also known as leader peptidases) remove the signal peptides from secretory proteins. In prokaryotes three types of SPases are known: type I (gene lepB) which is responsible for the processing of the majority of exported pre-proteins; type II (gene lsp) which only process lipoproteins, and a third type involved in the processing of pili subunits.

SPase I (EC 3.4.21.89) is an integral membrane protein that is anchored in the cytoplasmic membrane by one (in Bacillus subtilis) or two (in Escherichia coli) N-terminal transmembrane domains with the main part of the protein protuding in the periplasmic space. Two residues have been shown [[cite:PUB00002718], [cite:PUB00002224]] to be essential for the catalytic activity of SPase I: a serine and an lysine.

SPase I is evolutionary related to the yeast mitochondrial inner membrane protease subunit 1 and 2 (genes IMP1 and IMP2) which catalyse the removal of signal peptides required for the targeting of proteins from the mitochondrial matrix, across the inner membrane, into the inter-membrane space [[cite:PUB00005177]].

In eukaryotes the removal of signal peptides is effected by an oligomeric enzymatic complex composed of at least five subunits: the signal peptidase complex (SPC). The SPC is located in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. Two components of mammalian SPC, the 18 Kd (SPC18) and the 21 Kd (SPC21) subunits as well as the yeast SEC11 subunit have been shown [[cite:PUB00003576]] to share regions of sequence similarity with prokaryotic SPases I and yeast IMP1/IMP2.

;

This entry represents a conserved region of unknown biological significance which is located in the C-terminal section of S26 peptidases (SPase I and IMP1/2).

Name: Mitochondrial inner membrane protease subunit 2
ShortDescription: This entry represents the mitochondrial inner membrane protease (IMP) subunit 2 (MEROPS identifier S26.012). IMP removes an N-terminal targeting signal from a protein synthesized in the mitochondrial matrix but destined for export across the membrane to the mitochondrial inter-membrane space. IMP is a hetero-oligomer containing two homologous subunits that are both serine endopeptidases (IMP1 and IMP2) plus SOM1 [[cite:PUB00087534]]. IMP1 and IMP2 have overlapping specificities [[cite:PUB00061709]].

Name: Cystine knot, C-terminal
ShortDescription: Four recent crystal structures of growth factors--nerve growth factor, transforming growth factor-beta, platelet-derived growth factor, and human chorionic gonadotropin--from four separate superfamilies revealed that these proteins are structurally related and share a common overall topology [[cite:PUB00000890]]. These proteins have very little sequence homology, but they all have an unusual arrangement of six cysteines linked to form a "cystine-knot" conformation. The active forms of these proteins are dimers, either homo- or heterodimers [[cite:PUB00000091]]. Because of their shape, there appears to be an intrinsic requirement for the cystine-knot growth factors to form dimers. This extra level of organisation increases the variety of structures built around this simple structural motif [[cite:PUB00001089]].

Name: Sclerostin/Sclerostin domain-containing protein 1
ShortDescription: This sclerostin family consists of sclerostin and sclerostin domain-containing protein 1. Sclerostin (SOST) is thought to suppress bone formation. Mutations of the SOST gene lead to sclerosteosis, a progressive sclerosing bone dysplasia with an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. Radiologically, it is characterised by a generalised hyperostosis and sclerosis leading to a markedly thickened and sclerotic skull, with mandible, ribs, clavicles and all long bones also being affected. Due to narrowing of the foramina of the cranial nerves, facial nerve palsy, hearing loss and atrophy of the optic nerves can occur. Sclerosteosis is clinically and radiologically very similar to van Buchem disease, mainly differentiated by hand malformations and a large stature in sclerosteosis patients [[cite:PUB00011469]]. Sclerostin domain-containing protein 1, also known as USAG1, is a bone morphogenetic protein antagonist [[cite:PUB00059216]].

Name: Zinc/iron permease
ShortDescription:
The ZIP family consists of zinc transport proteins and many putative metal transporters found in al cellular organisms, including the Arabidopsis thaliana ZIP protein family which is responsible for zinc uptake in the plant [[cite:PUB00008168]]. ZIP proteins play essential roles in metal metabolism/homeostasis and are widely involved in numerous physiological and pathological processes.

The crystal structure of a ZIP from Bordetella bronchiseptica showed eight transmembrane helices (TMs) forming a tightly associated helix bundle, where four TMs create an inner bundle surrounded by the other four TMs and a a binuclear metal centre (BMC) is harboured in the transport pathway [[cite:PUB00103883]]. The two associated metal binding sites in the BMC play different roles: one of them is the key transport site, whereas the other, the auxiliary site, is required not only to achieve maximal zinc transport activity but also to maintain a uniform activity in a broad pH range [[cite:PUB00103882]].

ZIP4, a human member of this family, is related to a rare autosomal recessive disease caused by the inability to absorb sufficient zinc [[cite:PUB00103884]]. ZIPCO, a Plasmodium member, has a crucial role in the parasite liver-stage development [[cite:PUB00153751]].

Name: Latexin-type cystatin domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the Latexin-type cystatin domain.

Latexin (LXN), or tissue carboxypeptidase inhibitor (TCI), is the only known mammalian carboxypeptidase inhibitor (CPI). It is expressed in a cell type-specific manner in both central and peripheral nervous systems in the rat [[cite:PUB00012913]]. LTX has no detectable sequence similarity with plant and parasite inhibitors, but it is related to a human putative tumor suppressor protein, TIG1 ([swissprot:P49788]). TIG1 is larger than latexin, and the additional residues are thought to encode a membrane anchor at the N terminus. Other proteins with sequence identity to LXN are found in chicken (Ovocalyxin-32, [swissprot:Q90YI1]) and Xenopus, but no related proteins were found in nonvertebrates. Chicken Ovocalyxin-32 is a protein involved in egg shell production [[cite:PUB00032277], [cite:PUB00039699]].

The structure of LXN ([pdbe:1WNH]) shows no structural relationship with other CPIs. Furthermore, despite a lack of detectable sequence duplication, the structure incorporates two topologically analogous domains related by pseudo two-fold symmetry. Each domain comprises a curved five-stranded antiparallel β-sheet wrapped around an α-helix. These domains share a cystatin fold architecture found in proteins that inhibit cysteine proteases, suggesting an evolutionary and possibly functional relationship. LXN may have evolved from an ancestral cystatin-like protein as a consequence of a gene duplication event. The LXN-type cystatin domains are packed against each other through the helices and linked by a connecting segment encompassing a third α-helix. The two domains are arranged so that there is a cleft in this part of the structure that can accommodate a peptide chain [[cite:PUB00032277], [cite:PUB00039699]].

Name: Latexin
ShortDescription: This family consists of several animal specific latexin and proteins related to latexin that belong to MEROPS proteinase inhibitor family I47, clan I- [[cite:PUB00014133]].

Name: Proteasome assembly chaperone 3
ShortDescription: Proteasome assembly chaperone 3 (PSMG3) promotes assembly of the 20S proteasome [[cite:PUB00044884]]. It may cooperate with PSMG1-PSMG2 heterodimers to orchestrate the correct assembly of proteasomes.

Name: Proteasome Assembly Chaperone
ShortDescription: This superfamily of proteins is involved in the assembly and regulation of the 20S proteasome, a key component of the ubiquitin-proteasome system responsible for protein degradation. Members of this superfamily function as chaperones that facilitate the correct folding and assembly of proteasome subunits. They may work in conjunction with other specific chaperone proteins to ensure the proper formation of the proteasome's alpha-ring structure, which is crucial for its proteolytic activity. The superfamily plays a significant role in maintaining cellular homeostasis by participating in the degradation of misfolded or damaged proteins and the regulation of various protein pathways.

Name: TMEM120A/B
ShortDescription: This entry represents a group of transmembrane proteins including TACAN (also known as TMEM120A) and TMEM120B. TMEM120A is involved in mechanosensation and plays an essential role in lipid metabolism and adipocyte differentiation [[cite:PUB00094220], [cite:PUB00158954]]. It was first described as an ion channel that contributes to sensing mechanical pain [[cite:PUB00094219]], however, several studies show that TMEM120A does not exhibit mechanosensitive channel activity and display no typical ion channel structural characteristics [[cite:PUB00158955], [cite:PUB00158956], [cite:PUB00158957]]. TMEM120A is structurally similar to a lipid-modifying enzyme, ELOVL7, and contains a bound coenzyme A molecule, which suggests it might function as an enzyme in lipid metabolism [[cite:PUB00158955], [cite:PUB00158956], [cite:PUB00158957]]. Therefore, if TMEM120A is an enzyme rather than an ion channel is still in debate. TMEM120A and TMEM120B may be required for efficient adipogenesis [[cite:PUB00094220]].

Name: CARD11, CARD domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the CARD domain found in CARD11, also known as CARMA1. CARMA1, together with BCL10 (B-cell lymphoma 10) and Malt1 (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue-lymphoma-translocation gene 1), form the L-CBM signalosome (CBM complex in lymphoid immune cells) which mediates activation of NF-kB and MAPK by ITAM-coupled receptors expressed on immune cells. CARMA1 associates with BCL10 via a CARD-CARD interaction [[cite:PUB00064076]].

;

In general, CARDs are death domains (DDs) found associated with caspases [[cite:PUB00014109]]. They are known to be important in the signaling pathways for apoptosis, inflammation, and host-defense mechanisms [[cite:PUB00005464]]. DDs are protein-protein interaction domains found in a variety of domain architectures. Their common feature is that they form homodimers by self-association or heterodimers by associating with other members of the DD superfamily including PYRIN and DED (Death Effector Domain). They serve as adaptors in signaling pathways and can recruit other proteins into signaling complexes [[cite:PUB00082062]].

Name: Fanconi anaemia protein FANCD2
ShortDescription:
The Fanconi Anemia (FA) pathway is responsible for interstrand crosslink DNA repair [[cite:PUB00070095]]. The name originates the recessive syndrome known as Fanconi anemia, which causes developmental problems and cancer predisposition [[cite:PUB00070096]]. In this pathway, the FANCI-FANCD2 (ID) complex is ubiquitinated by the FA core complex and then travels to sites of damage to coordinate repair [[cite:PUB00070098], [cite:PUB00070099]]. FA pathway activation seems to trigger dissociation of FANCD2 from FANCI, coinciding with FANCD2 monoubiquitination which precedes monoubiquitination of FANCI [[cite:PUB00070101]]. This suggests a functional separation for FANCD2 from FANCI [[cite:PUB00070102]].

Monoubiquitinated FANCD2 functions to recruit DNA repair factors FAN1 (Fanconi-associated nuclease 1) [[cite:PUB00070097]] and SLX4 [[cite:PUB00070100]], suggesting that chromatin-bound FANCD2Ub is a docking platform for certain DNA repair nucleases. FANCD2 has also a role in replication fork recovery [[cite:PUB00070103]].

Name: Large ribosomal subunit protein bL9, N-terminal domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the large ribosomal subunit protein bL9. In Escherichia coli, bL9 is known to bind directly to the 23S rRNA. It belongs to a family of ribosomal proteins grouped on the basis of sequence similarities [[cite:PUB00001252]].

The crystal structure of Bacillus stearothermophilus bL9 shows the 149-residue protein comprises two globular domains connected by a rigid linker [[cite:PUB00007073]]. Each domain contains an rRNA binding site, and the protein functions as a structural protein in the large subunit of the ribosome. The C-terminal domain consists of two loops, an α-helix and a three-stranded mixed parallel, anti-parallel β-sheet packed against the central α-helix. The long central α-helix is exposed to solvent in the middle and participates in the hydrophobic cores of the two domains at both ends.

Name: Large ribosomal subunit protein bL9m, N-terminal domain
ShortDescription:
This domain is found at the N-terminal of human Large ribosomal subunit protein bL9m (MRP-L9) and similar proteins specific to vertebrates. MRP-L9 is a structural component of the large subunit of the ribosome [[cite:PUB00089007], [cite:PUB00089008], [cite:PUB00090386], [cite:PUB00154377]]. It shows two β-sheets connected by a loop [[cite:PUB00160049]].

;

Ribosomes are the particles that catalyse mRNA-directed protein synthesis in all organisms. The codons of the mRNA are exposed on the ribosome to allow tRNA binding. This leads to the incorporation of amino acids into the growing polypeptide chain in accordance with the genetic information. Incoming amino acid monomers enter the ribosomal A site in the form of aminoacyl-tRNAs complexed with elongation factor Tu (EF-Tu) and GTP. The growing polypeptide chain, situated in the P site as peptidyl-tRNA, is then transferred to aminoacyl-tRNA, and the new peptidyl-tRNA, extended by one residue, is translocated to the P site with the aid of the elongation factor G (EF-G) and GTP as the deacylated tRNA is released from the ribosome through one or more exit sites [[cite:PUB00007068], [cite:PUB00007069]]. About 2/3 of the mass of the ribosome consists of RNA and 1/3 consists of protein. The proteins are named in accordance with the subunit of the ribosome which they belong to: the small (S1 to S31) and the large (L1 to L44). Usually they decorate the rRNA cores of the subunits.

Many ribosomal proteins, particularly those of the large subunit, are composed of a globular, surfaced-exposed domain with long finger-like projections that extend into the rRNA core to stabilise its structure. Most of the proteins interact with multiple RNA elements, often from different domains. In the large subunit, about 1/3 of the 23S rRNA nucleotides are at least in van der Waals' contact with protein, and L22 interacts with all six domains of the 23S rRNA. Proteins S4 and S7, which initiate assembly of the 16S rRNA, are located at junctions of five and four RNA helices, respectively. In this way, proteins serve to organise and stabilise the rRNA tertiary structure. While the crucial activities of decoding and peptide transfer are RNA-based, proteins play an active role in functions that may have evolved to streamline the process of protein synthesis. In addition to their function in the ribosome, many ribosomal proteins have some function 'outside' the ribosome [[cite:PUB00007069], [cite:PUB00007070]].

ShortDescription:

Name: Large ribosomal subunit protein bL9m, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a presumed domain found at the C-terminal of the large ribosomal subunit protein bL9m (mitochondrial) from animals. This domain may adopt a similar fold to that of prokaryotic large ribosomal subunit protein bL9.

Name: Large ribosomal subunit protein bL9/RNase H1, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
The N-terminal domain of the large ribosomal subunit protein bL9 (previously known as ribosomal protein L9) is a regulatory RNA-binding module that binds to 23rRNA. bL9 is composed of two domains and functions as a structural protein in the large subunit of the ribosome.

The N-terminal domain of eukaryotic RNase HI, which is lacking in retroviral and prokaryotic enzymes, shows a striking structural similarity to the bL9 N-terminal domain, and may also function as a regulatory RNA-binding module. Eukaryotic RNases HI possess either one or two copies of the small N-terminal domain, in addition to the well-conserved catalytic RNase H domain. RNase HI belongs to the family of ribonuclease H enzymes that recognise RNA:DNA hybrids and degrade the RNA component.

Name: PA domain superfamily
ShortDescription: The PA (Protease associated) domain is found as an insert domain in diverse proteases, which include the MEROPS peptidase families A22B, M28, and S8A [[cite:PUB00003579]]. The PA domain is also found in some plant vacuolar sorting receptors and members of the RZF family, including [swissprot:O43567]. It has been suggested that this domain forms a lid-like structure that covers the active site in active proteases, and is involved in protein recognition in vacuolar sorting receptors [[cite:PUB00019976]].

Name: ER degradation-enhancing alpha-mannosidase-like protein 1/2/3
ShortDescription: This entry represents a group of alpha-1,2-specific exomannosidases that are involved in endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD), including EDEM1/2/3 from humans, Mnl1 from yeasts and MNS4/5 from Arabidopsis. Mnl1 forms a complex with Pdi1 to process unfolded protein-bound Man8GlcNAc2 oligosaccharides to Man7GlcNAc2, promoting degradation in unfolded protein response [[cite:PUB00096761]]. In humans, mannose trimming from Man8GlcNAc2 to Man7GlcNAc2 is performed mainly by EDEM3 and to a lesser extent by EDEM1, while EDEM2 catalyses the first mannose trimming step from Man9GlcNAc2 [[cite:PUB00086758]]. EDEM1 has been shown to recognise and deliver misfolded proteins to the SEL1L-containing ERAD complex [[cite:PUB00096762]]. MNS4/5 function in the formation of unique N-glycan structures that are specifically recognized by components of the endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) machinery, which leads to the degradation of misfolded glycoproteins [[cite:PUB00096763]].

Name: EDEM3, PA domain
ShortDescription:
EDEM3 is involved in endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD). It accelerates the glycoprotein degradation by catalyzing mannose trimming from Man8GlcNAc2 to Man7GlcNAc2 in the N-glycans [[cite:PUB00086758]].

;

This entry represents the PA (protease associated) domain of EDEM3. The function of this domain is not clear.

Name: Glycoside hydrolase family 47
ShortDescription:
O-Glycosyl hydrolases ([ec:3.2.1.]) are a widespread group of enzymes that hydrolyse the glycosidic bond between two or more carbohydrates, or between a carbohydrate and a non-carbohydrate moiety. A classification system for glycosyl hydrolases, based on sequence similarity, has led to the definition of 85 different families [[cite:PUB00004870], [cite:PUB00005266]]. This classification is available on the CAZy (CArbohydrate-Active EnZymes) website.

;

Glycoside hydrolase family 47 [cazy:GH47] comprises enzymes with only one known activity; alpha-mannosidase ([ec:3.2.1.113]).

Alpha-mannosidase is involved in the maturation of Asn-linked oligo-saccharides [[cite:PUB00002897]]. The enzyme hydrolyses terminal 1,2-linked alpha-D-mannose residues in the oligo-mannose oligosaccharide man(9)(glcnac)(2) in a calcium-dependent manner. The mannose residues are trimmed away to produce, first, man(8)glcnac(2), then a man(5)(glcnac)(2) structure.

Name: PA domain
ShortDescription: The PA (Protease associated) domain is found as an insert domain in diverse proteases, which include the MEROPS peptidase families A22B, M28, and S8A [[cite:PUB00003579]]. The PA domain is also found in a plant vacuolar sorting receptor [swissprot:O22925] and members of the RZF family, e.g. [swissprot:O43567]. It has been suggested that this domain forms a lid-like structure that covers the active site in active proteases, and is involved in protein recognition in vacuolar sorting receptors [[cite:PUB00019976]].

Name: Six-hairpin glycosidase-like superfamily
ShortDescription:
This domain superfamily contains up to seven α-hairpins arranged in closed circular array.

;

The biosynthesis of disaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides involves the action of hundreds of different glycosyltransferases. These enzymes catalyse the transfer of sugar moieties from activated donor molecules to specific acceptor molecules, forming glycosidic bonds. A classification of glycosyltransferases using nucleotide diphospho-sugar, nucleotide monophospho-sugar and sugar phosphates ([ec:2.4.1.-]) and related proteins into distinct sequence-based families has been described [[cite:PUB00009409]]. This classification is available on the CAZy (CArbohydrate-Active EnZymes) website. The same three-dimensional fold is expected to occur within each of the families. Because 3-D structures are better conserved than sequences, several of the families defined on the basis of sequence similarities may have similar 3-D structures and therefore form 'clans'.

Name: Seven-hairpin glycosidases
ShortDescription:
Glycoside hydrolase family 47 [cazy:GH47] comprises enzymes with only one known activity; alpha-mannosidase ([ec:3.2.1.113]).

Alpha-mannosidase is involved in the maturation of Asn-linked oligo-saccharides [[cite:PUB00002897]]. The enzyme hydrolyses terminal 1,2-linked alpha-D-mannose residues in the oligo-mannose oligosaccharide man(9)(glcnac)(2) in a calcium-dependent manner. The mannose residues are trimmed away to produce, first, man(8)glcnac(2), then a man(5)(glcnac)(2) structure.

Name: Exportin 4/7-like
ShortDescription:
This entry includes Ran-binding protein 17 from humans and similar proteins.

;

Exportins bind cargo molecules in the nuclei and transport them through nuclear pores to the cytoplasm, a process that requires RanGTP. XPO7 mediates the nuclear export of proteins with broad substrate specificity. They bind cooperatively to its cargo and to the GTPase Ran in its active GTP-bound form [[cite:PUB00095478], [cite:PUB00090434]].

Name: KATNB1-like protein 1
ShortDescription: Microtubule-severing enzyme Katanin is composed of a catalytic p60 subunit (A subunit, KATNA1) and a regulatory p80 subunit (B subunit, KATNB1). KATNBL1 functions as a regulator of Katanin A subunit microtubule-severing activity during mitosis [[cite:PUB00092939]].

Name: Katanin p80 subunit, C-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the C-terminal domain of katanin 80kDa subunit.

;

Katanin is a microtubule-severing protein consist of a 60kDa ATPase subunit (katanin-p60) and a 80kDa subunit (katanin-p80) [[cite:PUB00067483]], [cite:PUB00148635]]. Katanin-p80 is composed of an N-terminal WD40 repeat domain, a central proline-rich domain and a C-terminal domain required for dimerisation with the catalytic katanin-p60 [[cite:PUB00148635]]. The katanin complex associates with a specific subregion of the mitotic spindle leading to increased microtubule disassembly and targeting of katanin-p60 to the spindle poles [[cite:PUB00062074], [cite:PUB00058183], [cite:PUB00067482]]. Katanin is a crucial regulator of early embryonic development, and recessive mutations or deletions in the KATNB1 gene cause severe microcephaly or microlissencephaly [[cite:PUB00148635]]. Katanin forms a complex with another microcephaly-associated protein, ASPM (abnormal spindle-like microcephaly-associated) that controls spindle pole organization, poleward spindle flux, and spindle positioning, processes that when misregulated could perturb proliferation of neuronal progenitors and lead to microcephaly. Katanin also interacts with CAMSAPs (calmodulin-regulated spectrin-associated proteins) and is required for limiting the length of CAMSAP-bound MT minus-end stretches during interphase [[cite:PUB00148635]]. In plants it also plays an important role as it is required for the bending of the plant axis toward the light source.

Name: MAGT1/OST3/OST6
ShortDescription:
During N-linked glycosylation of proteins, oligosaccharide chains are assembled on the carrier molecule dolichyl pyrophosphate in the following order: 2 molecules of N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc), 9 molecules of mannose, and 3 molecules of glucose. These 14-residue oligosaccharide cores are then transferred to asparagine residues on nascent polypeptide chains in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). As proteins progress through the Golgi apparatus, the oligosaccharide cores are modified by trimming and extension to generate a diverse array of glycosylated proteins [[cite:PUB00054185], [cite:PUB00020140]].

The oligosaccharyl transferase complex (OST complex) [ec:2.4.1.119] transfers 14-sugar branched oligosaccharides from dolichyl pyrophosphate to asparagine residues [[cite:PUB00008612]]. The complex contains nine protein subunits: Ost1p, Ost2p, Ost3p, Ost4p, Ost5p, Ost6p, Stt3p, Swp1p, and Wbp1p, all of which are integral membrane proteins of the ER. The OST complex interacts with the Sec61p pore complex [[cite:PUB00054184]] involved in protein import into the ER.

This entry represents subunits OST3 and OST6. OST3 is homologous to OST6 [[cite:PUB00008613]], and several lines of evidence indicate that they are alternative members of the OST complex. Disruption of both OST3 and OST6 causes severe underglycosylation of soluble and membrane-bound glycoproteins and a defect in the assembly of the complex. Hence, the function of these genes seems to be essential for recruiting a fully active complex necessary for efficient N-glycosylation [[cite:PUB00008613]]. This entry also includes the magnesium transporter protein 1, also known as OST3 homologue B, which might be involved in N-glycosylation through its association with the oligosaccharyl transferase (OST) complex.

Name: Nonsense-mediated mRNA decay protein 3
ShortDescription: This entry includes nonsense-mediated mRNA decay protein 3 (Upf3) and its homologues. In budding yeasts, Upf3 is involved in the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway [[cite:PUB00090013]]. Human Upf3a and Upf3b are components of the exon-junction complex (EJC), which promotes nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) and regulate translation efficiency [[cite:PUB00084767]].

Name: UPF3 domain
ShortDescription:
Nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) is a surveillance mechanism by which eukaryotic cells detect and degrade transcripts containing premature termination codons. Three 'up-frameshift' proteins, UPF1, UPF2 and UPF3, are essential for this process in organisms ranging from yeast, human to plants [[cite:PUB00007740]]. Exon junction complexes (EJCs) are deposited ~24 nucleotides upstream of exon-exon junctions after splicing. Translation causes displacement of the EJCs, however, premature translation termination upstream of one or more EJCs triggers the recruitment of UPF1, UPF2 and UPF3 and activates the NMD pathway [[cite:PUB00015577], [cite:PUB00015578]].

This entry contains UPF3. The crystal structure of the complex between human UPF2 and UPF3b, which are, respectively, a MIF4G (middle portion of eIF4G) domain and an RNP domain (ribonucleoprotein-type RNA-binding domain) has been determined to 1.95A. The protein-protein interface is mediated by highly conserved charged residues in UPF2 and UPF3b and involves the β-sheet surface of the UPF3b ribonucleoprotein (RNP) domain, which is generally used by these domains to bind nucleic acids. In UPF3b the RNP domain does not bind RNA, whereas the UPF2 construct and the complex do. It is clear that some RNP domains have evolved for specific protein-protein interactions rather than as nucleic acid binding modules [[cite:PUB00015595]].

Name: Protein spinster-like
ShortDescription: The entry includes Drosophila protein spinster [[cite:PUB00097040]], its vertebrate homologues, and the MFS-type efflux pumps from bacteria. Humans contain three homologues called protein spinster homologues 1 (SPNS1), 2 (SPNS2), and 3 (SPNS3). Protein spinster and its homologues may be sphingolipid transporters that play central roles in endosomes and/or lysosomes storage. SPNS2 is also called sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) transporter and is required for migration of myocardial precursors. S1P is a secreted lipid mediator that plays critical roles in cardiovascular, immunological, and neural development and function [[cite:PUB00097043], [cite:PUB00097042], [cite:PUB00097041]]. These proteins belong to the Major Facilitator Superfamily (MFS) of membrane transport proteins, which are thought to function through a single substrate binding site, alternating-access mechanism involving a rocker-switch type of movement. Also included in this family are the probable sphingolipid transporter spinster homologues 1-3 from Arabidopsis thaliana.

Name: Growth hormone-inducible transmembrane protein
ShortDescription: GHITM (also known as MICS1) appears to be ubiquitiously expressed in mammalian cells and expression has also been observed in various cancer cell lines [[cite:PUB00086371]]. It is involved in maintenance of mitochondrial morphology and apoptotic release of cytochrome c [[cite:PUB00086374]]. It is closely related to the BAX inhibitor (BI)-1 like family of small transmembrane proteins, which have been shown to have an anti-apoptotic effect [[cite:PUB00086370], [cite:PUB00086372], [cite:PUB00086373]].

Name: Bax inhibitor 1-related
ShortDescription:
This entry represents BI-1 and related sequences, including lifeguard proteins, which resemble BI-1 and also act as apoptotic regulators [[cite:PUB00098575]].

This entry also includes bacterial and viral proteins, related to human BAX inhibitor 1, such as Transmembrane protein HWLF3 from human cytomegalovirus, a glycoprotein that contributes to immune evasion by promoting lysosomal degradation of the host stress-inducible NKG2D ligand MICA, thereby diminishing natural killer (NK) cell activation [[cite:PUB00162443]].

;

Bax inhibitor-1 (BI-1) [[cite:PUB00001966]] is a suppressor of apoptosis that interacts with BCL2 and BCL-X. Human Bax BI-1 is an evolutionarily conserved integral membrane protein containing multiple membrane-spanning segments localised to the ER membrane. It has 6-7 membrane-spanning domains. The C termini of the mammalian BI-1 proteins are comprised of basic amino acids resembling some nuclear targeting sequences, but otherwise the predicted proteins lack motifs that suggest this function. BI-1 also regulates cell death triggered by ER stress [[cite:PUB00053809], [cite:PUB00098575], [cite:PUB00098576]]. BI-1 appears to exert its effect through an interaction with calmodulin [[cite:PUB00053810]]. Crystal structure of a bacterial member reveals that these proteins mediate a calcium leak across the membrane in a pH-dependent manner. Calcium homoeostasis balances passive calcium leak with active calcium uptake. The structure exists in a pore-closed and pore-open conformation, at pHs of 8 and 6 respectively [[cite:PUB00098576], [cite:PUB00095242]].

Name: U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 10, N-terminal
ShortDescription: This entry represents the N-terminal domain of Utp10, which is a HEAT-repeat containing protein involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA [[cite:PUB00008496]]. Utp10 is also involved in 40S ribosome maturation [[cite:PUB00090010]]. Proteins containing this domain also include HEATR1 from humans. HEATR1 is required for optimal pre-ribosomal RNA transcription by RNA polymerase I [[cite:PUB00090011]].

Name: Utp10/HEAT1, HEAT-repeats domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a HEAT-repeats domain found in HEATR1, Utp10 and similar eukaryotic proteins.

;

Proteins in this entry contain an armadillo-type fold, and a BP28, C-terminal domain. It includes HEAT repeat -containing protein 1 (HEATR1) from human and its orthologues from fungi, U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 10 (Utp10), which is a HEAT-repeat containing protein involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA [[cite:PUB00008496]]. Utp10 is also involved in 40S ribosome maturation [[cite:PUB00090010]]. HEATR1 is a ribosome biogenesis factor required for recruitment of Myc to nucleoli [[cite:PUB00158858], [cite:PUB00151110]]. It is involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA and it is required for optimal pre-ribosomal RNA transcription by RNA polymerase I [[cite:PUB00090011]]. HEATR1 plays a role in neuronal-lineage cell proliferation [[cite:PUB00158858]].

Name: BP28, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found in the C-terminal of BAP28 proteins [[cite:PUB00016366]] (which are involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA and ribosome biosynthesis [[cite:PUB00043646]]) and in other BAP28-like proteins.

Name: U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 10
ShortDescription: Proteins in this entry contain an armadillo-type fold, and a BP28, C-terminal domain. It includes HEAT repeat -containing protein 1 (HEATR1) from human and its orthologues from fungi, U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 10 (Utp10), which is a HEAT-repeat containing protein involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA [[cite:PUB00008496]]. Utp10 is also involved in 40S ribosome maturation [[cite:PUB00090010]]. HEATR1 is a ribosome biogenesis factor required for recruitment of Myc to nucleoli [[cite:PUB00158858], [cite:PUB00151110]]. It is involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA and it is required for optimal pre-ribosomal RNA transcription by RNA polymerase I [[cite:PUB00090011]]. HEATR1 plays a role in neuronal-lineage cell proliferation [[cite:PUB00158858]].

Name: PDZD7, Harmonin N-like domain
ShortDescription: Human PDZ domain-containing protein 7 (PDZD7) is a scaffolding protein which associates with the Usher Syndrome protein network, and localizes to the stereocilia Ankle-link. Usher syndrome is the leading cause of genetic deaf-blindness. PDZD7 has a role as in Usher syndrome type 2 (and not in USH1) in humans. Whirlin, Usherin and GRP98 are other USH2 proteins. The latter two form the ankle links and whirlin is thought to be a scaffold for protein interactions at these links. PDZD7, whirlin, and harmonin (an USH1 protein) have a similar domain composition [[cite:PUB00093324], [cite:PUB00093325]]. The domain represented here is a putative protein-binding module based on its sequence similarity to the N-terminal domain of harmonin [[cite:PUB00048309]]. Cooperative effects of mutations in PDZD7 and Usherin, and in PDZD7 and GPR98, result in a digenic USH2 phenotype [[cite:PUB00093326]].

Name: Anthrax toxin receptor, C-terminal
ShortDescription:
Anthrax is an acute disease in humans and animals, which is caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis. While the disease can be lethal, there are effective vaccines against anthrax, and some forms of the disease respond well to antibiotic treatment.

The anthrax toxin consists of the proteins protective antigen (PA), lethal factor (LF) and oedema factor (EF). The first step of toxin entry into host cells is the recognition by PA of a receptor on the surface of the target cell. The subsequent cleavage of receptor-bound PA enables EF and LF to bind and form a heptameric PA63 pre-pore, which triggers endocytosis. PA has been shown to bind to two cellular receptors, termed anthrax toxin receptor 1 (ANTXR1/TEM8) and 2 (ANTXR2). Both bind to PA with high affinity and are capable of mediating toxicity [[cite:PUB00031351], [cite:PUB00022677]], and both are type 1 membrane proteins that include an approximately 200-aa extracellular von Willebrand factor A (VWA) domain with a metal ion-dependent adhesion site (MIDAS) motif [[cite:PUB00022677]].

;

This region is found in the putatively cytoplasmic C terminus of the anthrax receptor.

This entry represents the anthrax toxin receptors. Their physiologic function is unclear. ANTXR1/TEM8 seems to have a role in arteriogenesis [[cite:PUB00088335]].

This region is found in the putatively extracellular N-terminal half of the anthrax receptor. It is probably part of the Ig superfamily and most closely related to [interpro:IPR002909].

Name: tRNA endonuclease ANKZF1/VMS1
ShortDescription: This entry represents a group of proteins predominantly found in eukaryotes, including Ankyrin repeat and zinc finger domain-containing protein 1 from human (ANKZF1) and VMS1 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae which belong to the VLRF1 (Vms1-Like Release Factor-1) clade [[cite:PUB00091190]]. They have been identified as peptidyl-tRNA hydrolases that release nascent chains from stalled ribosomes [[cite:PUB00091190]]. ANKZF1, VMS1 orthologue in human, plays a role in the cellular response to hydrogen peroxide and in the maintenance of mitochondrial integrity under conditions of cellular stress [[cite:PUB00102007]]. VMS1 is a component of an evolutionarily conserved system for ubiquitin-mediated mitochondria-associated protein degradation (MAD), which is necessary to maintain mitochondrial, cellular, and organismal viability. It is involved in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated degradation (ERAD) pathway [[cite:PUB00077110], [cite:PUB00102008]].

Name: VLRF1/Vms1
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a domain found in proteins belonging to the VLRF1 clade of the archaeo-eukaryotic RF1 (aeRF1) superfamily. The yeast Vms1 is the founding member the VLRF1 (Vms1-Like Release Factor-1) clade. In addition to the eukaryotic orthologs of Vms1 the VLRF1 clade also contains members from certain bacteria, predominantly bacteroidetes and more divergent versions in certain Archaea [[cite:PUB00091190]].

Proteins containing this domain have a conserved glutamine residue in the release factor catalytic loop, suggesting they function as active peptidyl-tRNA hydrolases at the ribosome [[cite:PUB00091190]].

This domain is also found in Ankyrin repeat and zinc finger domain-containing protein 1 from humans (ANKZF1), which plays a role in the cellular response to hydrogen peroxide and in the maintenance of mitochondrial integrity under conditions of cellular stress [[cite:PUB00102007]]. It is an endonuclease that cleaves polypeptidyl-tRNAs downstream of the ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) pathway to release incompletely synthesized polypeptides for degradation [[cite:PUB00151173], [cite:PUB00091190], [cite:PUB00151172]].

Name: Vms1-associating treble clef domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the treble clef fold domain found at C terminus of many, but not all, Vms1/ANKZF1-like proteins [[cite:PUB00091190]].

Name: WD repeat-containing protein 54, beta-propeller
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the β-propeller domain WD repeat-containing protein 54 (WDR54) from human and similar eukaryotic sequences.

;

WDR54 has a regulatory effect on ERK signaling pathway activity in response to EGF stimulation, when is cross-linked to form dimers and trimers. It colocalizes with the EGF receptor in a WDR54-specific vesicle where it sustains the internalisation and controls the degradation of the EGF receptor after EGF stimulation [[cite:PUB00151666]].

Name: Conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 4
ShortDescription: COG4 is a component of the conserved oligomeric Golgi (COG) complex which mediates the proper glycosylation of proteins trafficking through the Golgi apparatus. It is a member of the CATCHR (complexes associated with tethering containing helical rods) family, which includes components of the exocyst, COG, GARP, and Dsl1 complexes, sharing structural and functional features: the α-helical bundles at the middle/C-terminal and a N-terminal coiled-coil region [[cite:PUB00100076], [cite:PUB00100040]].

Name: COG4 transport protein, middle alpha-helical bundle
ShortDescription: COG4 is a component of the conserved oligomeric Golgi (COG) complex which mediates the proper glycosylation of proteins trafficking through the Golgi apparatus. It is included in the CATCHR (complexes associated with tethering containing helical rods) family, which includes components of the exocyst, GARP, and DSL1 complexes and share structural and functional features: the α-helical bundles at the middle/C-terminal (described as domains A-D/E) and a N-terminal coiled-coil region [[cite:PUB00017118], [cite:PUB00100040], [cite:PUB00100047]]. This domain is found in the middle region of COG4 and corresponds to domains B and C. Mutations in COG4 cause fatal congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDGs) in humans [[cite:PUB00053070], [cite:PUB00100076]].

Name: Conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 4, C-terminal
ShortDescription:
This is the C-terminal domain of COG4, which contains the key Arginine residue that stabilises this domain and it is required for the proper glycosylation of cell surface proteins [[cite:PUB00053070], [cite:PUB00100076]].

;

ShortDescription:
This is the N-terminal coiled-coil of COG4.
